summary.text: Factoring the relevant binomial series under the Cartier operator, together with equidistribution of binomial coefficients modulo residue classes mod 3, makes the first two correction terms vanish and expresses the one-step difference as a sum over indices \(j\ge3\). Antipalindromic coefficient symmetry, repeated summation by parts, and Kummer–Legendre valuation bounds make every summand divisible by \(p^{3v_p(M)+3}\), which gives the result for \(M=np^{k-1}\); the exceptional parameter case is handled by an explicit period-six closed form.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}=1+x+2x^2+5x^3+\cdots .
\]
For an integer \(m\), define
\[
a_m(N)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}[x^r]c(x)^{mN}.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is \(a(N)=a_4(N)\). We prove the stronger assertion
\[
a_m(np^k)\equiv a_m(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}
\tag{1}
\]
for every integer \(m\), every prime \(p\ge5\), and positive integers \(n,k\). All binomial coefficients below are generalized binomial coefficients
\[
\binom{z}{r}=\frac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-r+1)}{r!}\qquad(z\in\mathbb Z,r\ge0).
\]
They are integers, including for negative \(z\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. A coefficient form for the truncated Catalan sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Lagrange inversion applied to \(c=1+xc^2\) gives, for \(r\ge1\),
\[
[x^r]c(x)^s=\frac{s}{s+r}\binom{s+2r-1}{r}.
\tag{2}
\]
When the denominator is nonzero, the absorption identity
\[
(r+1)\binom Nr+1=(N-r)\binom Nr
\tag{3}
\]
shows that (2) can also be written
\[
[x^r]c(x)^s
 =\binom{s+2r-1}{r}-\binom{s+2r-1}{r-1}.
\tag{4}
\]
Indeed, with \(N=s+2r-1\), (3), used at \(r-1\), says
\[
(s+r)\binom N{r-1}=r\binom Nr,
\]
and (4) follows after multiplication by \(s+r\).

Introduce the integer sequence
\[
g_0=1,
\qquad
 g_r=\begin{cases}2,&r>0\text{ and }3\mid r,\\-1,&r>0\text{ and }3\nmid r,
\end{cases}
\tag{5}
\]
and define
\[
P(A,N)=\sum_{r=0}^{N}g_r\binom A{N-r}.
\tag{6}
\]
The key elementary telescoping identity is
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{N}[x^r]c(x)^s=P(s+2N,N),
\tag{7}
\]
provided none of the denominators \(s+r\), \(1\le r\le N\), vanishes.

Here is a proof. The sequence \(g_r\) satisfies
\[
g_t+g_{t+1}+g_{t+2}=0\qquad(t\ge1).
\tag{8}
\]
Reflecting the sum in (6), and using (8), gives
\[
P(A,N)+P(A,N+1)+P(A,N+2)
 =\binom A{N+2}-\binom A N.
\tag{9}
\]
Only the boundary terms survive; at the boundary one uses \(g_0=1,g_1=-1\). Pascal's identity also gives
\[
P(B+1,N+1)=P(B,N+1)+P(B,N).
\tag{10}
\]
Combining (9) and (10) yields the step identity
\[
P(A+2,N+1)-P(A,N)
 =\binom{A+1}{N+1}-\binom{A+1}{N}.
\tag{11}
\]
Starting at \(N=0\), where both sides of (7) are 1, and applying (4) and (11) proves (7) by induction.

Take now \(s=mN\). If \(m\ne-1\), then
\[
mN+r\ne0\qquad(1\le r\le N).
\]
Indeed either \(m\ge0\), when the left side is positive, or \(m\le-2\), when it is at most \(-2N+N<0\). Consequently
\[
a_m(N)=P((m+2)N,N)
       =\sum_{r=0}^{N}g_r\binom{(m+2)N}{N-r}
       \qquad(m\ne-1).
\tag{12}
\]

Let
\[
G(X)=\sum_{r\ge0}g_rX^r.
\]
Equation (8), together with the first coefficients, is equivalently
\[
(1+X+X^2)G(X)=1-X^2.
\tag{13}
\]
For an integer \(A\) and a power series \(\Phi\), put
\[
L(\Phi;A,M)=[X^M](1+X)^A\Phi(X),
\qquad
u(A,M)=L(G;A,M).
\tag{14}
\]
Reflecting the convolution in (14) shows from (12) that
\[
a_m(M)=\nu((m+2)M,M)\qquad(m\ne-1).
\tag{15}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The Cartier operator and two basic vanishings
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix a prime \(p\ge5\). For \(1\le r\le p-1\), set
\[
q_r=\frac1p\binom pr,
\]
and put \(q_0=q_p=q_{p+1}=\cdots=0\). These are integers because \(p\mid\binom pr\) in the indicated range. Let
\[
Q(X)=\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}q_rX^r.
\tag{16}
\]
For a series \(F=\sum f_rX^r\), write
\[
\mathcal C_pF=\sum_{r\ge0}f_{pr}X^r,
\qquad
\mathcal I_pF=F(X^p).
\tag{17}
\]
The elementary convolution identity
\[
\mathcal C_p\bigl(F(X^p)H(X)\bigr)=F(X)\mathcal C_pH(X)
\tag{18}
\]
follows simply by observing that in the coefficient of \(X^{pN}\), a term from \(F(X^p)\) has index \(pi\), leaving index \(p(N-i)\) in \(H\).

We need
\[
\mathcal C_pG=G,
\qquad
\mathcal C_p(QG)=0,
\qquad
\mathcal C_p(Q^2G)=0.
\tag{19}
\]
The first identity follows from (5): because \(p\ne3\), one has \(3\mid pr\) if and only if \(3\mid r\), and the constant terms also agree.

We now prove the other two identities. For a residue \(\rho\pmod3\), define
\[
S_N(\rho)=\sum_{\substack{0\le r\le N\\r\equiv\rho\ (3)}}\binom Nr.
\tag{20}
\]
Pascal's identity gives
\[
S_{N+1}(\rho)=S_N(\rho)+S_N(\rho-1).
\tag{21}
\]
Since the three residue classes exhaust all indices,
\[
S_N(\rho)+S_N(\rho-1)+S_N(\rho-2)=2^N.
\]
Applying (21) three times therefore yields
\[
S_{N+3}(\rho)=3\cdot2^N-S_N(\rho).
\tag{22}
\]
The initial triples are
\[
(S_1(0),S_1(1),S_1(2))=(1,1,0),
\quad
(S_2(0),S_2(1),S_2(2))=(1,2,1).
\]
A prime \(p\ge5\) has \(p\equiv1\) or \(2\pmod3\); moreover \(p\) is odd. Iterating (22), and distinguishing these two residues, gives
\[
3S_p(\rho)=2^p-2+3[\rho=0]+3[\rho=p],
\tag{23}
\]
where brackets denote indicator functions and residues are modulo 3. Removing the endpoint terms \(r=0,p\) from (23) gives the residue-independent identity
\[
3\sum_{\substack{1\le r\le p-1\\r\equiv\rho\ (3)}}\binom pr=2^p-2.
\tag{24}
\]
On the other hand
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\binom pr=2^p-2.
\tag{25}
\]

For \(N\ge p\), the coefficient of \(X^N\) in \(QG\), multiplied by \(p\), is
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{p-1}\binom pr g_{N-r}.
\]
All \(N-r\) here are positive. By (5), this equals three times the sum of \(\binom pr\) over the one residue class \(r\equiv N\pmod3\), minus the unrestricted sum. It is zero by (24) and (25). Thus
\[
[X^N]QG=0\qquad(N\ge p).
\tag{26}
\]
In particular every coefficient selected by \(\mathcal C_p\), except possibly the constant one, vanishes; the constant one vanishes because \(Q(0)=0\). Hence \(\mathcal C_p(QG)=0\).

For later use we also need the reflection law
\[
[X^r]QG=-[X^{p-r}]QG\qquad(0\le r\le p).
\tag{27}
\]
To see this without another binomial sum, use (13). If \(R_r=[X^r]QG\), then
\[
R_{t+2}+R_{t+1}+R_t=q_{t+2}-q_t.
\tag{28}
\]
Also \(q_{p-r}=q_r\), by the symmetry of binomial coefficients. Therefore
\(D_r=R_r+R_{p-r}\) satisfies
\[
D_r+D_{r-1}+D_{r-2}=0,
\quad D_r=D_{r-3}.
\]
The endpoint values are \(D_0=D_p=0\), by \(Q(0)=0\) and (26). Since \(p\equiv1\) or \(2\pmod3\), these endpoint conditions and the three-term recurrence force \(D_0=D_1=D_2=0\), hence every \(D_r=0\). This proves (27).

Now consider \(\mathcal C_p(Q^2G)\). For a selected coefficient of index \(pN\), write it as the convolution of \(Q\) with \(QG\). If \(N\ge2\), every potentially nonzero \(q_r\) leaves index \(pN-r\ge p\), so (26) makes every term zero. For \(N=0\) the constant coefficient is zero. For \(N=1\), pair the term indexed by \(r\) with that indexed by \(p-r\). The equality \(q_{p-r}=q_r\) and the antisymmetry (27) make each pair cancel. Thus the third identity in (19) follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The transfer formula
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let
\[
T(X)=(1+X)^{-1},
\qquad
\rho(X)=Q(X)T(X^p).
\tag{29}
\]
The binomial theorem gives
\[
(1+X)^p=1+X^p+pQ(X).
\]
Since \((1+X^p)T(X^p)=1\), this factors as
\[
(1+X)^p=(1+X^p)(1+p\rho(X)).
\tag{30}
\]
Raising (30) to an arbitrary integer power \(z\) gives the formal-series identity
\[
(1+X)^{zp}=(1+X^p)^z(1+p\rho(X))^z.
\tag{31}
\]
For negative \(z\), this remains valid because all involved series have constant term 1 and are therefore invertible.

Define
\[
\Psi_j(X)=\mathcal C_p(\rho(X)^jG(X)).
\tag{32}
\]
By (18), (19), and \(\rho=QT(X^p)\),
\[
\Psi_0=G,
\qquad \Psi_1=0,
\qquad \Psi_2=0.
\tag{33}
\]
Indeed, for example,
\[
\mathcal C_p(\rho G)=T\,\mathcal C_p(QG)=0,
\]
and similarly for \(j=2\).

Take the coefficient of \(X^{pM}\) in (31) multiplied by \(G\), then apply (18), and expand \((1+p\rho)^A\) binomially. Only finitely many terms can affect a fixed coefficient. One obtains
\[
\nu(Ap,pM)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{pM}\binom Ajp^jL(\Psi_j;A,M).
\tag{34}
\]
By (33), the \(j=0\) term is \(\nu(A,M)\), while the terms \(j=1,2\) vanish. Hence
\[
\nu(Ap,pM)-\nu(A,M)
 =\sum_{j=3}^{pM}\binom Ajp^jL(\Psi_j;A,M).
\tag{35}
\]
Our task is therefore to prove strong divisibility term by term.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Structure of \(\Psi_j\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Put
\[
H_j(X)=Q(X)^jG(X),
\qquad W_{j,r}=[X^{pr}]H_j(X).
\tag{36}
\]
From (29), (18), and \(T^j=(1+X)^{-j}\),
\[
\Psi_j(X)=(1+X)^{-j}\mathcal C_pH_j(X).
\tag{37}
\]
Consequently
\[
L(\Psi_j;AM,M)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{M}\binom{AM-j}{M-r}W_{j,r}.
\tag{38}
\]

The coefficients of \(H_j\) satisfy the antipalindromic law
\[
[X^N]H_j=-[X^{jp-N}]H_j
\qquad(j\ge1,N\ge0).
\tag{39}
\]
For \(j=1\), this is (27), together with (26) outside the interval \([0,p]\). Suppose it holds for \(j\). Since \(H_{j+1}=QH_j\), reflect the convolution using \(q_{p-r}=q_r\); paired terms cancel by the induction hypothesis. The support facts needed at the ends are elementary: \(Q^j\) has no term below degree \(j\), and (26), followed inductively by convolution with \(Q\), gives
\[
[X^N]H_j=0\quad\text{if }N<j\text{ or }N>j(p-1).
\tag{40}
\]
This proves (39) for all \(j\).

In particular
\[
W_{j,r}=-W_{j,j-r},
\qquad W_{j,0}=0,
\qquad W_{j,r}=0\ (r\ge j).
\tag{41}
\]
Define negative partial sums
\[
S_r=-\sum_{t=0}^{r}W_{j,t}.
\tag{42}
\]
The total sum \(\sum_{t=0}^jW_{j,t}\) is zero by (41). Reflecting a prefix against the complementary suffix therefore gives
\[
S_r=S_{j-1-r}.
\tag{43}
\]
Moreover
\[
S_r=0\quad(r>j-1),
\tag{44}
\]
and the lower support in (40) gives
\[
S_r=0\quad\left(r<1+\left\lfloor\frac{j-1}{p}\right\rfloor\right).
\tag{45}
\]
Finally (42) says
\[
W_{j,r}=S_{r-1}-S_r,
\tag{46}
\]
with the natural convention at \(r=0\), where both sides are zero.

Substitute (46) into (38) and perform finite summation by parts. Since the boundary values vanish, one gets
\[
L(\Psi_j;AM,M)=\mathcal L(A,M,S,j-1),
\tag{47}
\]
where, for a sequence \(V\) supported on \([0,w]\),
\[
\mathcal L(A,M,V,w)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{M}V_r
 \left\{
 \binom{AM-w-1}{M-r-1}-\binom{AM-w-1}{M-r}
 \right\}.
\tag{48}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. A generalized Kummer estimate
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write \(v_p(N)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in a positive integer \(N\). We need the following estimate. If \(b<a\), \(b>0\), then
\[
p^{v_p(M)}\mid (a-1)!\binom{AM-a}{M-b}
\tag{49}
\]
for every integer \(A\).

We justify (49). Put \(E=v_p(M)\). For a nonnegative upper index \(N\), Kummer's theorem says that
\[
v_p\binom NK
\]
is the number of carries when \(K\) and \(N-K\) are added in base \(p\). Equivalently, a carry occurs at level \(p^i\) exactly when
\[
p^i\le (K\bmod p^i)+((N-K)\bmod p^i).
\tag{50}
\]
Legendre's formula says
\[
v_p((a-1)!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{a-1}{p^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{51}
\]
For each \(1\le i\le E\), either \(p^i\le a-1\), in which case level \(i\) contributes at least one to (51), or \(a\le p^i\). In the latter case, because \(p^i\mid M\), one has
\[
(M-b)\bmod p^i=p^i-b.
\]
If the upper index is \(N=AM-a\ge0\), then
\[
(N-(M-b))\bmod p^i=p^i-(a-b),
\]
so the sum of these two residues is at least \(p^i\), and (50) supplies a carry. Thus every \(i\le E\) contributes either to the factorial valuation or to the binomial valuation.

If \(AM-a<0\), use
\[
\binom{-d}{r}=(-1)^r\binom{d+r-1}{r}.
\tag{52}
\]
For the reflected nonnegative upper index, the relevant complementary residue is \(a-1\), and it again combines with \(p^i-b\) to produce the needed carry whenever the factorial does not already contribute. If \(M-b\) exceeds the nonnegative upper index, the binomial coefficient is zero. If \(b\ge M\), then \(M-b=0\), while \(M\mid(a-1)!\) because \(0<M\le a-1\). These cases prove (49) completely.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The descent divisibility
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(E=v_p(M)\), and suppose \(M>0\). We prove the following statement by strong induction on \(w\): if

* \(V_r=V_{w-r}\) for every \(r\),
* \(V_r=0\) for \(r>w\),
* there is a \(t_0\ge1\) such that \(V_r=0\) for \(r<t_0\), and
* \(w<p^E\),

then
\[
p^{2E}\mid
p^{v_p(w!)+v_p((w-1)!)}\mathcal L(A,M,V,w).
\tag{53}
\]

If \(w<2t_0\), symmetry and the lower support condition force every \(V_r\) to vanish, so (53) is immediate. Assume therefore \(w\ge2t_0\).

Set
\[
P_1=\sum_{r=0}^{M}V_r\binom{AM-w}{M-r}.
\tag{54}
\]
The basic generalized-binomial identity
\[
s\left(\binom{s-1}{k}-\binom{s-1}{k+1}\right)
 =(2k+2-s)\binom s{k+1}
\tag{55}
\]
follows from Pascal's identity and (3). Apply it term by term in (48), with \(s=AM-w\). The factor on the right splits as
\[
2(M-r)-(AM-w)=-(A-2)M+(w-2r).
\]
Define
\[
\widetilde W_r=(w-2r)V_r,
\qquad
V'_r=-\sum_{t=0}^{r}\widetilde W_t.
\tag{56}
\]
Because \(V\) is palindromic, \(\widetilde W\) is antipalindromic. Hence its total sum is zero, and its negative partial sums \(V'\) are palindromic about \((w-1)/2\), supported on \([t_0,w-1]\). Summation by parts gives the exact recursion
\[
(AM-w)\mathcal L(A,M,V,w)
 =-(A-2)MP_1+\mathcal L(A,M,V',w-1).
\tag{57}
\]

Apply (49), with \(a=w\) and \(b=r\), to every nonzero term of (54). The endpoints vanish by the support assumptions. We obtain
\[
p^E\mid (w-1)!P_1.
\tag{58}
\]
Let
\[
G_0=v_p((w-1)!),\qquad v=v_p(w).
\]
Cancelling the exact \(p^{G_0}\)-part of \((w-1)!\) in (58) gives
\[
p^{E-G_0}\mid P_1
\tag{59}
\]
when \(G_0\le E\), while if \(G_0>E\) this assertion is vacuous. Since \(p^E\mid M\), (59) implies in either case
\[
p^{2E}\mid p^{2G_0}(A-2)MP_1.
\tag{60}
\]

The induction hypothesis applied to \(V'\) and \(w-1\) gives
\[
p^{2E}\mid
p^{v_p((w-1)!)+v_p((w-2)!)}
\mathcal L(A,M,V',w-1).
\tag{61}
\]
Now
\[
v_p(w!)=v+G_0.
\tag{62}
\]
Multiplying (57) by \(p^{v_p(w!)+G_0}=p^{v+2G_0}\), equations (60) and (61) show that its right side is divisible by \(p^{v+2E}\). Thus
\[
p^{v+2E}\mid(AM-w)\,p^{v_p(w!)+G_0}\mathcal L(A,M,V,w).
\tag{63}
\]
Because \(w<p^E\) and \(p^E\mid M\), subtraction from the multiple \(AM\) does not change the exact valuation:
\[
v_p(AM-w)=v_p(w)=v.
\tag{64}
\]
Indeed \(p^v\) divides both terms, while divisibility by \(p^{v+1}\) of their difference would, since \(v<E\), force \(p^{v+1}\mid w\), a contradiction. Cancelling this exact factor \(p^v\) in (63) proves (53).

Taking \(w=j-1\), \(V=S\) from (42), and using (43)--(45) and (47), gives, whenever \(j\ge3\) and \(j-1<p^E\),
\[
p^{2E}\mid
p^{F_j}L(\Psi_j;AM,M),
\quad
F_j=v_p((j-1)!)+v_p((j-2)!).
\tag{65}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Divisibility of every term in the transfer sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We claim that for every \(j\ge3\),
\[
p^{3E+3}\mid
\binom{AM}{j}p^jL(\Psi_j;AM,M),
\qquad E=v_p(M).
\tag{66}
\]

First, the absorption identity in the form
\[
j\binom{AM}{j}=AM\binom{AM-1}{j-1}
\tag{67}
\]
shows that \(p^E\mid j\binom{AM}{j}\). Removing the factor of \(j\) prime to \(p\), we get
\[
p^E\mid p^{v_p(j)}\binom{AM}{j}.
\tag{68}
\]

There are two cases.

Case 1: \(j-1<p^E\). Then (65) and (68), multiplied together, supply \(p^{3E}\). The remaining explicit power \(p^j\) supplies at least three more factors because
\[
v_p(j)+F_j+3\le j.
\tag{69}
\]
To prove (69), use Legendre's bound
\[
(p-1)v_p(r!)<r
\]
for \(r>0\). Since \(p-1\ge4\), apply it to \(j!\) and \((j-2)!\), and use
\(v_p(j!)=v_p(j)+v_p((j-1)!)\). The resulting two strict inequalities immediately imply (69). This proves (66) in Case 1.

Case 2: \(p^E\le j-1\). Here no divisibility of \(L\) is needed. We have
\[
v_p(j)+2E+3\le j.
\tag{70}
\]
Indeed the elementary induction \(4r+1\le5^r\), together with \(p\ge5\), gives
\[
4E+1\le5^E\le p^E\le j-1.
\]
Similarly, because \(p^{v_p(j)}\le j\),
\[
4v_p(j)+1\le j.
\]
These two inequalities imply (70). Combining (70) with (68), the surplus power in \(p^j\) contributes at least \(2E+3\) beyond the \(p^{v_p(j)}\) already used in (68). Thus the total is at least \(p^{3E+3}\), proving (66) in Case 2 as well.

It follows from (35), term by term, that
\[
\nu(Ap,pM)-\nu(A,M)\equiv0\pmod {p^{3v_p(M)+3}}.
\tag{71}

--------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Completion for \(m\ne-1\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let
\[
M=np^{k-1},
\qquad A=(m+2)M.
\]
Then \(Mp=np^k\), and by (15)
\[
a_m(np^k)=\nu(Ap,Mp),
\qquad
a_m(np^{k-1})=\nu(A,M).
\]
Since \(p^{k-1}\mid M\), we have \(v_p(M)\ge k-1\). Therefore
\[
3v_p(M)+3\ge3k.
\]
Equation (71) proves (1) for every \(m\ne-1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
9. The exceptional parameter \(m=-1\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Although this case is not needed for A333096, it completes the stronger theorem. The denominator in (2) vanishes at the final summand when \(s=-N,r=N\), so it must be treated separately. That final coefficient is zero, while the preceding terms telescope as before, giving for \(N\ge1\)
\[
a_{-1}(N)=P(N-2,N-1).
\tag{72}
\]
The step identity (11), with \(A=N-2\), shows
\[
P(N-2,N-1)=P(N,N)+1.
\tag{73}
\]
Using \(\binom N{N-r}=\binom Nr\) in (6), and the definition (5), one finds
\[
P(N,N)=3S_N(0)-2^N-1.
\]
Thus
\[
a_{-1}(N)=3S_N(0)-2^N.
\tag{74}
\]
Applying (22) twice gives
\[
3S_{N+6}(0)-2^{N+6}=3S_N(0)-2^N.
\tag{75}
\]
The six values for residues \(0,1,2,3,4,5\pmod6\) are respectively
\[
2,1,-1,-2,-1,1.
\tag{76}
\]
Hence \(a_{-1}(N)\) depends only on \(N\pmod6\), through the even function on residues displayed in (76).

A prime \(p\ge5\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(5=-1\pmod6\). Multiplication by \(p\) therefore either preserves a residue modulo 6 or negates it. The values in (76) are unchanged under negation. Consequently
\[
a_{-1}(pN)=a_{-1}(N)
\]
exactly, and (1) follows trivially in this exceptional case.

We have proved (1) for every integer \(m\). Taking \(m=4\) gives the sequence A333096, and therefore, for every prime \(p\ge5\) and positive integers \(n,k\),
\[
\boxed{a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}}.
\]
